prompt: What did Ana do before DuckDB could answer a question about the orders file in the lake?

choices.text: Copied the file into a folder in the lake, as it was
choices.why: Right. DuckDB read it in place and worked out the types from its contents.

choices.text: Created a table and loaded the file
choices.why: No table was created; that is the warehouse's way.

choices.text: Converted it to Parquet so that any engine could read it
choices.why: It stayed a CSV.

choices.text: Registered it in a catalogue
choices.why: Nothing was registered; that is part of how a swamp starts.

prompt: Which of these does the section count as the lake's offer? Choose all that apply.

choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Cheap storage for any kind of file
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Many engines reading the same files
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Every file checked against a model on arrival

prompt: A warehouse checks data when it is loaded: schema on write. A lake leaves it to each reader: schema on ___.
With `union_by_name = true`, the query over both files returned 586,584 orders and no error. What was wrong with it?

choices.text: It counted the old file twice, once under each column name
choices.why: The count is the old 577,468 plus the new week.

choices.text: The shipping column was summed as text and came out as zero
choices.why: That query did not sum shipping.

choices.text: The new week's orders all lost their customer, which sat in client_id
choices.why: Right. Its customer was in `client_id`, a column the query never named.

choices.text: DuckDB silently dropped the rows whose types did not match
choices.why: No rows were dropped; a column was left empty.

prompt: Of 586,584 orders, 430,221 had a customer. How many orders had none?
A job writing twenty Parquet files to a plain folder dies after the eleventh. What do readers see?

choices.text: Nothing until the job is rerun, because the folder is locked
choices.why: A folder has no lock.

choices.text: Eleven files, as if complete
choices.why: Right. A partial load looks like a whole one.

choices.text: An error on read
choices.why: Nothing knows which files were meant to be there.

choices.text: The previous version of the data, restored by the storage service
choices.why: Object storage does not know which files make a version.

hint: Five of the six in the section.

prompt: What does an open table format add to a folder of Parquet files?

choices.text: A server that every reader and writer connects to
choices.why: Delta needs no server; the lab ran none.

choices.text: A new file format that replaces Parquet
choices.why: The data stays ordinary Parquet.

choices.text: An index of every row's position in every file
choices.why: It lists files and their statistics, not rows.

choices.text: A log of commits
choices.why: Right. Each commit says which files it added and removed.

prompt: Why does a job that dies halfway through a Delta write leave no partial table?
hint: What does a reader read first?

choices.text: The library deletes the files it wrote when the process ends
choices.why: A process that dies cleans nothing up.

choices.text: Object storage rolls the folder back to its state before the job
choices.why: Object storage knows nothing about the job.

choices.text: Its new files were never named in a commit, and readers follow only the log
choices.why: Right. Readers follow the log, so uncommitted files are invisible.

choices.text: Each file is written inside its own database transaction
choices.why: There is no database; there is a log.

prompt: Match each format to where it came from.
Ana wrote 404,067 rows of 2024 and 483,410 of 2025. How many rows does the table hold after commit 1?
Which part of the folder is the table, rather than the data?

choices.text: The JSON files in _delta_log, one per commit
choices.why: Right. Without them the folder is a pile of Parquet.

choices.text: The folders named year=2024 and year=2025
choices.why: Those are partitions, and the log records them too.

choices.text: The Parquet files, because their footers list the schema
choices.why: A Parquet file knows only itself.

choices.text: The newest Parquet files
choices.why: Newest is not current: after an update the old file stays beside the new one.

prompt: Put the actions of Ana's commit 0 in the order they appear in the file.
hint: Who wrote it comes first; the data file last.
trap: `add` last: the file joins a table whose schema the earlier lines have already declared.

prompt: Two writers try to create commit 2 at the same moment. What happens?
hint: A commit is one file appearing.

choices.text: Both succeed
choices.why: Only one file can be commit 2.

choices.text: The table is locked until an administrator chooses one of them
choices.why: Nobody has to choose; the storage does.

choices.text: The later one overwrites the earlier one's commit file
choices.why: Creating the file is atomic, so the second finds it taken.

choices.text: One wins; the other rereads and retries
choices.why: Right. No server is needed between them.

prompt: A table with thousands of commits writes a ___ now and then, a Parquet file with the state as of that commit, so readers need not replay from zero.
Ana's update changed 1 row and copied 404,066. How many rows did the new 2024 file hold?
Why did a one-row correction copy 404,066 rows?

choices.text: Delta rewrites every file in the table on every commit, to keep statistics exact
choices.why: The 2025 file was not touched.

choices.text: Copy on write rewrites the file
choices.why: Right. The file holding the row was read and written again whole.

choices.text: The predicate matched the whole year because order ids repeat each year
choices.why: One row was updated.

choices.text: The library made a backup copy before changing anything
choices.why: The old file is the backup; it was left where it was.

prompt: What do deletion vectors change about a delete?

choices.text: They record row positions to ignore, and leave the rewrite for a later compaction
choices.why: Right. The rewrite waits for a compaction.

choices.text: They remove the rows from the file in place, without rewriting it
choices.why: A Parquet file is not edited in place.

choices.text: They delete the old file from disk at once, so no vacuum is needed
choices.why: Nothing is deleted from disk by a commit.

choices.text: They make every reader rewrite the file the first time it reads it
choices.why: Readers skip the positions; they do not rewrite.

prompt: Which is the last version of Ana's table that still has the till error?

choices.text: Version 2, the current one, because the old file is still on disk
choices.why: Version 2 reads the corrected file.

choices.text: None of them
choices.why: Old versions keep their files.

choices.text: Version 1, the one before the update
choices.why: Right. 9,574,389,852, before the correction.

choices.text: Version 0
choices.why: It has the error, but version 1 is later and has it too.

prompt: After a real vacuum with zero retention, which versions of Ana's table can still be read?

choices.text: All three
choices.why: The log lists a file that no longer exists.

choices.text: Only version 2
choices.why: Right. Versions 0 and 1 both need the original 2024 file.

choices.text: Versions 1 and 2, because version 0 had no 2025 file
choices.why: Version 1 needs the original 2024 file too.

choices.text: None, until the table is rewritten from the warehouse
choices.why: The current version's files are kept.

prompt: A customer asks to be forgotten and is deleted from a Delta table today. When are they gone from the disk?

choices.text: Today, when the delete is committed
choices.why: The commit only stops listing the old files.

choices.text: Never, because Delta keeps every version for ever by design
choices.why: Vacuum exists to remove them.

choices.text: When the next checkpoint is written, since it replaces the log
choices.why: A checkpoint summarises the log; it deletes no data file.

choices.text: After a vacuum
choices.why: Right. Until then old versions still hold the rows.

prompt: Ana appended a row with 13 columns to a 12-column Delta table without `schema_mode`. What did the history show afterwards?

choices.text: A commit 3 marked as failed, with the error message
choices.why: Refused writes leave no commit at all.

choices.text: A commit 3 that dropped the extra column and appended the rest
choices.why: Nothing was appended.

choices.text: Still ending at commit 2: the write was refused before any commit
choices.why: Right. The write was refused before the commit.

choices.text: A commit 3 adding the column, with no rows
choices.why: That needs `schema_mode="merge"`.

prompt: Which of these would a Delta table's schema check stop? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A batch with an extra column
choices.why: Yes, as the capture showed.

choices.text: A batch with text where a number is declared
choices.why: Yes, a type mismatch.

choices.text: Prices in reais written into a column meant for centavos
choices.why: Same type, wrong meaning: it passes.

choices.text: A renamed source column already mapped to the table's own name
choices.why: The table sees its own name: it passes.

prompt: What does choosing Iceberg over Delta change in the star of lessons 2 to 6?

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right. The formats differ in metadata; facts and dimensions are the same.

choices.text: Dimensions must be stored as manifests rather than tables
choices.why: Manifests list data files; they are not a modelling choice.

choices.text: Type 2 history moves into the format's time travel
choices.why: Time travel is about table versions, not about when a customer moved.

choices.text: Surrogate keys are replaced by Iceberg's column ids
choices.why: Column ids name columns, not rows.

choices.text: Bronze, so the raw file is corrected as soon as it lands
choices.why: Bronze keeps the file as received.

choices.text: Gold
choices.why: Then the fix would be repeated per table.

choices.text: In each dashboard's query
choices.why: That is the swamp's way: every reader separately.

choices.text: Silver
choices.why: Right. Every reader after it sees one name.

prompt: A nightly job overwrites a Delta table's 2025 partition. On Tuesday a report reads wrong numbers; Wednesday's load already ran. What answers "what did Monday's report read?"
hint: Versions, and how long they last.

choices.text: Reading the raw files of the 2025 folder in order of their timestamps
choices.why: The folder holds files from several versions; only the log says which belonged together.

choices.text: Reading the version that was current on Monday
choices.why: Right, as long as no vacuum has removed its files.

choices.text: Rerunning Monday's load
choices.why: The source has moved on since Monday.

choices.text: Nothing, because an overwrite deletes the previous files immediately
choices.why: An overwrite is a commit; old files stay until a vacuum.

prompt: A team keeps raw CSVs in a bucket and every analyst cleans them in a notebook. Which change from this lesson fixes the most?

choices.text: A silver layer, cleaned once into tables with a schema, that every analyst reads
choices.why: Right. One clean-up, in a table with a schema.

choices.text: Converting the CSVs to Parquet in place, keeping the notebooks
choices.why: Faster reads; still one clean-up per analyst.

choices.text: Turning on versioning in the bucket so every file keeps its history
choices.why: History of files is not a table, and cleaning stays repeated.

choices.text: Moving the notebooks to a bigger cluster so clean-ups run faster
choices.why: Faster duplication is still duplication.
